title: Reactive Shino glaze application
subtitle: Applying a high-feldspar Shino glaze and reading the reduction marks, crawl, and carbon trapping
excerpt: Shino is a Japanese high-feldspar glaze known for its white-to-orange pitted surface, carbon trapping (dark marks where the thick glaze traps carbon from the kiln atmosphere), and crawling. The glaze is intentionally unpredictable: the pitting, crawl, and carbon variation are considered desirable. This tutorial covers a studio Shino recipe, correct application thickness, and how the kiln atmosphere produces the characteristic surface.
sourceNotes: Shino glaze base recipe and properties synthesised from studio ceramics glaze chemistry reference including Digitalfire, and historical Japanese Mino-ware Shino documentation. Carbon trapping mechanism is documented in wood-fire and reduction ceramics technical reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: The mechanism by which carbon from kiln smoke is absorbed into a very thick feldspar glaze before the glaze seals over. Creates dark marks and flashing on the Shino surface.
Movement of molten glaze away from an area during firing, leaving a bare clay surface. In Shino, controlled crawl is a surface character, not a defect.
Oxygen-poor kiln atmosphere that causes metal oxides to change colour. Essential for Shino carbon trapping and orange-flash effects.
A standardised measure of kiln heat-work. Shino matures at cone 9 to 10.

content.text: Glaze chemistry safety
Feldspar, silica, and kaolin are respirable crystalline silica hazards. Wear a P100 respirator (not N95) when weighing and mixing dry ingredients. Work in a ventilated space or outdoors.

The classic Shino recipe described here contains no metal colourants beyond the iron naturally present in the soda feldspar. When fired to cone 9 to 10, the base recipe falls within food-safe limit formula bounds. Do not add iron oxide, manganese, or other colourants without re-checking the limit formula.

Shino glaze is applied at 3 to 4 mm dry thickness: much thicker than standard glazes. This thickness produces significant running during firing. Apply kiln wash to all shelves below Shino pieces. Maintain a minimum 25 mm clear foot ring.
Shino is different from most glazes. Its best effects come from the glaze behaving badly. Dark
carbon trapping
crawl
texture, and orange flash are all wanted results. The thick glaze coat seals the clay surface early in the firing. Carbon from early
reduction
gets trapped under the sealed surface. Later in the firing the kiln switches to oxidation. The glaze turns white on top. The trapped carbon marks stay locked below.
Base recipe (1,000 g dry batch)

Classic American Shino base for cone 9 to 10 reduction firing. Mix: Nepheline syenite 500 g (or potash feldspar as a substitute). Soda feldspar 200 g. Kaolin 200 g. Silica 100 g. The fired surface is white to warm cream, matte, and slightly pitted.
Mixing the glaze

Wearing the P100 respirator: weigh and combine all dry ingredients. Add 500 to 600 ml water: Shino is applied much thicker than normal glazes, so the slurry should be considerably thicker than single cream: closer to double cream or even yoghurt consistency. Sieve through 60-mesh screen (not 80-mesh: Shino benefits from coarser particle size for the pitting effect).
Target specific gravity: 1.55 to 1.65: significantly higher than a standard glaze. Test on a scrap of bisque: the dry coat should be 3 to 4 mm thick and completely opaque.
Application
Apply to
bisque

by dipping. Hold the piece in the glaze for 5 to 6 seconds: much longer than a standard dip. The bisque must be thoroughly saturated with the thick glaze. Alternatively, brush three to four thick coats with a hake brush, each in a different direction, allowing each coat to dry before the next.

Shino must cover the entire piece uniformly: thin patches produce uneven carbon trapping and blotchy results. The glaze coat, when dry, should look like a thick white skin covering the form completely.
Clear a minimum 25 mm bare foot ring. This is essential: Shino runs substantially in the kiln. Load on kiln-washed shelves. Leave 25 mm space between adjacent pieces in the kiln.
Firing sequence for carbon trapping
Carbon trapping requires a specific reduction sequence. Begin reduction at
cone

012 (approximately 875 °C) and maintain until cone 08 (approximately 955 °C). This is the window in which the feldspar glaze begins to seal: the early reduction carbon is trapped beneath the sealing glaze surface. After cone 08, switch to neutral or light oxidation through peak temperature. The late-oxidation period converts the glaze surface to white while the trapped carbon remains locked below. More early reduction produces darker marks; less produces a cleaner white.

rows.problem: Shino fired to a uniform dull cream: no carbon trapping or pitting
rows.cause: Application too thin; or reduction started too late in the firing
rows.fix: Apply thicker (test for 3 to 4 mm dry coat). Begin reduction earlier: at cone 012 rather than cone 06.

rows.problem: Glaze ran off the foot ring and adhered to the kiln shelf
rows.cause: Foot ring not fully cleared; glaze applied too thick
rows.fix: Extend bare foot ring to 25 mm minimum. Test on a scrap tile at the same thickness before loading finished pieces.

rows.problem: Surface is smooth and featureless: no crawl or pitting
rows.cause: Glaze over-fired; or specific gravity too low
rows.fix: Reduce peak temperature by one cone. Mix a denser glaze (higher specific gravity).
